hints: Notice all four options are written as multiples of $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, the magnitude of charge on one electron or proton.
Recall that any isolated charge carrier must have net charge $Q = ne$ where $n$ is a positive or negative whole number.
Divide each listed charge by $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and look for the one that does not give a whole number for $n$.
walkthrough: Identify the elementary charge $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ from options C and D, which are $+1e$ and $+2e$.
State the quantisation rule: net charge on electrons and ions that carry current must be $Q = ne$, where $n = ...-2, -1, +1, +2...$ is an integer.
Test each option by calculating $n = Q/e$: A gives $-4.8/1.6 = -3$, C gives $+1.6/1.6 = +1$, D gives $+3.2/1.6 = +2$.
For the remaining value, $n = -2.4/1.6 = -1.5$, which is not an integer and so cannot occur as the net charge on a current carrier.

options.A: This is $-3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, a whole-number multiple of the elementary charge, so it can exist on an ion with excess electrons.
options.B: This is $-1.5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, not a whole-number multiple of the elementary charge, so it cannot be the net charge on a carrier.
options.C: This is $+1 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, equal to one elementary charge, as for a proton or positive ion that has lost one electron.
options.D: This is $+2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, a whole-number multiple of the elementary charge, so it can exist on a doubly ionised carrier.
